notes.meaning: The Lord tells Isaiah to take a large scroll or tablet and write on it with ordinary, readable handwriting. The name to write down means 'speed to the spoil, hurry to the plunder.' It announced publicly that Judah's enemies would soon be attacked and stripped of their wealth.

God appoints two respected, well-known men to serve as official witnesses. They would record the date and the written prophecy. When the predicted events took place, their testimony would prove that God had foretold it long before it happened.

Isaiah's wife conceives and gives birth to a son. God commands the prophet to name the boy Maher-shalal-hash-baz, the very name written on the public scroll. The child's life became a ticking clock for God's coming judgment.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some early church writers like John Chrysostom saw the prophetess as a type or shadow of the Virgin Mary, though traditional Catholic notes also acknowledge the literal wife of Isaiah.

notes.meaning: Before a toddler is old enough to say basic words like 'Father' or 'Mother,' which usually takes a year or two, the threat would end. The king of Assyria would invade and strip the wealth of Damascus in Syria and Samaria in northern Israel. This fulfilled God's promise to break the alliance that threatened Judah.

The Lord speaks again to warn the people who despised the gently flowing waters of Shiloah. That peaceful stream in Jerusalem represented God's quiet care and the gentle rule of David's royal line. Instead of trusting God, the people took delight in foreign kings and earthly alliances.

Because the people rejected God's quiet care, the Lord would bring a massive flood upon them. This flood represents the mighty king of Assyria and his vast, powerful army. Just as the Euphrates River bursts over its banks in flood season, Assyria would sweep across the land.

The Assyrian invasion would not stop in the north, but would surge into Judah until it reached neck-deep, threatening to drown the whole nation. Yet the capital of Jerusalem would remain above water, because the land belongs to Immanuel, which means 'God is with us.' God would not allow His promised kingdom to be completely destroyed.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern interpreters view the address to Immanuel here as ironic, suggesting God's presence would initially be felt as judgment rather than protection.

notes.meaning: Isaiah issues a bold challenge to all the hostile nations that plot against God's people. Even if they band together and arm themselves for battle, their efforts will fail. In the end, every enemy coalition will be shattered to pieces.

Foreign rulers might craft clever military strategies and issue royal decrees against Judah, but their schemes will come to nothing. Their plans cannot succeed because God is with His people. His presence guarantees that His promises will stand.

The Lord placed His strong hand upon Isaiah through a powerful touch of inspiration. God firmly warned the prophet not to adopt the mindset or copy the faithless habits of the crowd around him. Believers must not let popular opinion guide how they respond to crisis.

God commands His servants not to join the crowd in obsessing over political plots or treason. The people of Judah were terrified of foreign alliances and rushed to make deals with pagan powers. God's people must not live in dread of the things that terrify the world.

The Lord of Hosts—the commander of heaven's armies—is the only one people should regard as holy. Believers honor Him by relying completely on His power and faithfulness. True reverence for God removes the fear of earthly kings and armies.

To those who trust Him, the Lord is a sanctuary, a holy place of safety and peace. But to those who refuse to believe, He becomes an obstacle in the road—a stone that trips them up and a trap that catches them. Both the northern and southern kingdoms suffered ruin because they rejected Him.

differ.view: God secures His chosen people in Christ, while those who are not elect are appointed to stumble at the stone through their own unbelief.
People stumble because of their own free choice to reject the Messiah, though God's grace preserves a remnant who choose to trust Him.

notes.meaning: Many people will trip over this stone, fall down, and be broken. Like birds caught unexpectedly in a hunter's net, unbelievers who reject God will be trapped by their own rebellion. Turning away from the Lord leads to certain ruin.

differ.view: God ordained this stumbling so that He would protect His chosen elect while leaving hardened unbelievers to their appointed fall.
The statement that many would fall means the rejection was not total, and people stumbled because of their own choice to reject the Messiah.

notes.meaning: God directs that His prophetic revelation and law be wrapped up and sealed like an official scroll. Because the nation at large refused to listen, this truth was to be carefully guarded among Isaiah's faithful disciples. True believers preserve and treasure God's word when society abandons it.

Even though God seemed to be hiding His face and withdrawing His favor from Israel in judgment, Isaiah resolves to wait for Him. The prophet puts his whole trust in the Lord, confident that God will eventually show mercy to His people. Waiting on God means trusting His promises even in dark seasons.

Isaiah and his sons served as living signs to the nation from the Lord of Hosts on Mount Zion. Their prophetic names carried God's message: judgment on enemies, a returning remnant, and salvation from the Lord. Their faithful family life pointed ahead to Christ and His spiritual children.

When trouble struck, people urged each other to consult mediums and fortune-tellers who whispered and muttered spells. Isaiah shows how foolish this is: a nation should seek help from the living God, not ask the dead about matters concerning the living. Turning to the occult shows a tragic loss of faith.

God's law and His revealed message are the true test for every spiritual teaching. If any message does not agree with what God has spoken, it has no truth or spiritual light in it. Believers must test every voice against the Bible.

People who turn from God to false guides will wander through the land dejected and famished. As starvation and misery set in, they will become furious. Instead of repenting of their sins, they will look up and curse their earthly king and their God.

Finding no comfort from heaven, the rebellious people look down to the earth, but see only misery, black darkness, and crushing distress. Those who reject God's guidance are left without hope and driven out into total darkness. Sin ultimately leads to loneliness and despair.
